reviewedScope: City-specific examples derived from recorded source-backed fields, not new independent parcel approvals

thornton-co: Thornton's indoor six-square-foot rule differs from generic sizing

Thornton's official FAQ allows up to six hens at eligible detached single-family homes and requires at least six square feet of indoor coop floor for each hen. Six birds therefore need at least 36 square feet of usable coop floor. CoopCheck's generic planning rule of four square feet per bird would give 24 and must not be used as proof of local compliance.

A Thornton plan also needs a fenced backyard, one coop, a maximum coop area of 120 square feet and height of seven feet, and five-foot separation from side and rear property lines. The city says no standard chicken-keeping permit is required, but an attached townhouse does not meet the detached-home condition and other construction or HOA restrictions remain separate.
westminster-co: A quarter-acre flock tier also changes the coop area

Westminster's official animal-management rules allow up to six hens on detached-home lots of one-quarter acre or less, with higher flock tiers available for larger qualifying parcels. Its coop rule requires at least six square feet of indoor floor area per hen. A six-hen layout therefore needs at least 36 square feet; twelve hens require at least 72 under the same rule, before checking the permitted flock tier.

The city requires an approved backyard-livestock permit, currently listed at $25. Coop placement is limited to a screened rear yard at least ten feet from side and rear property lines, and other size and height limits apply. A large lot alone does not waive the permit or site-layout checks.
long-beach-ca: The fifth chicken changes both permits and dwelling distance

Long Beach provides a useful comparison between four and five chickens. The cited municipal code requires a separation of ten feet from an adjacent person's dwelling for one to four live chickens; for five to ten it rises to 35 feet, and five or more chickens require an animal-care permit. Eleven to twenty birds use a 50-foot dwelling-distance tier. These distances are to buildings, not simply to boundary fences.

The city separately calls for at least ten square feet of permeable outdoor containment per bird. Five chickens therefore imply at least fifty square feet of permeable enclosure. The general twenty-fowl maximum does not override the distance bands, zoning and additional permit requirements.
roseville-ca: Mixed species count together, and the run has a boundary setback

Roseville's reviewed city guidance groups ducks, chickens and pigeons under a ten-bird combined allowance. Six chickens and four ducks use all ten under that category rather than allowing ten birds of each species. Roosters are not categorically excluded by this allowance, but animal-noise rules still apply.

The city requires a 20-foot separation from property lines for chicken enclosures, including fenced runs. For an illustrative 45-foot-wide lot, the two opposing 20-foot bands leave only five feet of width before other restrictions; fitting an animal shelter could be impractical. The city's discretionary special permit for nonconforming locations is not automatic permission.
aurora-co: Six hens or eight depends on actual parcel size

Aurora's reviewed program normally allows up to six residential hens; a qualifying single-family residential lot of at least 20,000 square feet may keep up to eight. A 19,000-square-foot parcel cannot simply select eight hens because the coop is large. The city requires its chicken or duck permit before acquisition and prohibits residential roosters.

Housing must generally remain in the rear yard with at least fifteen feet of separation from abutting property boundaries unless the specific affected owners provide the written consent contemplated by the rule. That possibility does not waive other zoning restrictions. Draw the true lot lines and consent requirements before arranging the coop footprint.
longmont-co: A one-time hen permit does not authorize free-range placement

Longmont's standard nonagricultural allowance is four hens, and the reviewed city form requires a one-time chicken-hen permit. Roosters do not qualify for the routine residential program apart from narrow educational or scientific exceptions. A four-hen drawing should begin with the existing rear-yard structures, not just the count and suggested indoor area.

The city's application adds enclosure and separation rules for side and rear lot lines and nearby structures, plus specific exceptions. It also restricts free-ranging without relevant abutting-owner permission. An owner's written permission for an exception is not a substitute for the city permit; confirm the current form and actual parcel conditions before building.
tacoma-wa: Extra birds require more than a larger coop

Tacoma's ordinary adult-poultry allowance is six per parcel. A higher count toward ten requires specified written consent from qualifying nearby residence owners, not just more coop floor area. A homeowner planning eight hens should establish whether the additional-bird approval exists before buying materials.

Animal enclosures also have to remain behind the main building's front wall, outside required side-yard setbacks and at least twelve feet from certain dwelling or lodging buildings. Structures exceeding 200 square feet trigger the city's building-permit rule. That is not a promise that smaller structures ignore all zoning requirements.
yakima-wa: A four-hen count can pass while the coop location fails

Yakima's planning guidance describes up to four hens on eligible residential premises and excludes roosters. For a four-hen coop beside a garage, measure separately to the residential building, property lines and the other nearby structures. The cited rules require ten feet from a residence or property line, five feet from other structures and backyard confinement.

A coop can satisfy a generic space calculator yet be too close to a fence or a building. Some detached accessory structures have different permit thresholds, but that does not override chicken-specific placement regulations. Verify the residential zoning, site survey and construction category.
sacramento-ca: The actual yearly licensing calculation for three hens

Sacramento's current city page lists a maximum of three chickens per residential parcel and requires annual poultry licenses plus a coop permit. Using the published amounts, three $20 chicken licenses and one $47 coop permit add up to $107 in annual city poultry charges. Confirm current fees before applying because older downloadable documents have shown previous prices.

A qualifying coop belongs in the rear yard, between fifteen and forty-two square feet, and at least twenty feet from the nearest neighboring dwelling rather than a blanket twenty feet from every property line. The city also requires a roof, walls, nests and appropriate upkeep. A generic size calculation alone cannot verify this.
gresham-or: Three hens need two different distance measurements

Gresham's official guidance permits up to three adult hens on qualifying single-family properties, with a chicken permit required before keeping them; the posted fee is $50 for two years. A minimum two square feet of indoor coop floor per adult hen gives six square feet for three birds, but that statutory figure is not necessarily a comfortable winter housing target.

Both coop and run must be in the rear yard. The coop needs ten feet to a property line and twenty-five feet to a neighboring dwelling, while the run must also remain ten feet from lot lines. Overnight coop-confinement hours and HOA restrictions require independent attention.
kent-wa: A 7,000-square-foot lot changes the fowl count

Kent's official FAQ describes up to three domesticated fowl on a qualifying lot of 5,000 square feet, plus one for each additional 1,000 square feet. A qualifying 7,000-square-foot parcel therefore suggests up to five fowl under this arithmetic, subject to other conditions. The city's FAQ does not publish a categorical rooster ban, but noise and nuisance rules still matter.

The city also lists ten feet between a chicken coop and the property line. Its general shed guidance discusses building permits at 200 square feet or larger, but applying that threshold to a specific chicken house requires a building-classification check. Property easements may impose further siting restrictions.
beaverton-or: Lot size and tenant consent are separate requirements

Beaverton's cited law permits up to four hens on qualifying properties of at least 5,000 square feet containing a detached single-family home or duplex. For a renter on a qualifying 6,000-square-foot parcel, written permission from the property owner is still necessary; the sufficient lot size does not automatically replace that consent.

A coop cannot occupy the prohibited front-of-house area and has to satisfy the city's published distance from neighboring dwellings. That twenty-foot separation should not be confused with a universal twenty-foot setback from every fence. Confirm accessory-structure permits, the actual neighbor-building location and private HOA conditions separately.
mesa-az: Mesa's combined animals rule needs a parcel-specific reading

Mesa's recorded ordinance uses a combined count for fowl and certain small animals on the first half-acre. For example, six hens and four rabbits may use the ordinary ten-animal allowance, subject to exceptions and zoning. This is not a blanket permission for ten chickens plus ten rabbits or an automatic eligibility finding for any small backyard.

Mesa's cited 40-foot enclosure and 75-foot building-to-neighbor-residence provisions may be affected for qualifying small lots by Arizona state preemption. Those figures cannot be blindly treated as universal fence-line buffers. Determine which law controls the actual parcel and separately check unresolved building and animal permits.
tempe-az: A seventh hen raises a different use-permit question

Tempe's official zoning summary allows up to six domestic chickens on eligible residential lots. Adding a seventh cannot be justified merely by providing extra floor space: the city describes a use-permit process for exceeding the normal allowance. Roosters are restricted outside agricultural zoning, so replacing a hen with a rooster also changes the result.

For a site under one acre, Tempe's published rule limits chicken enclosure height relative to the property's fence or wall. This is a height restriction, not a universal numerical lot-line setback. Record the parcel zoning, enclosure height and proposed bird count before relying on any drawing.
salem-or: Salem measures some setbacks to buildings, not lot lines

Salem's reviewed residential poultry category allows up to twelve birds and says no routine keeping license is necessary. For an illustrative six-hen site in the rear yard, a keeper should identify each other building on the same parcel and the residential building on the next lot. The city cites three feet to other on-site buildings and twenty-five feet to a neighboring residence.

A large rear yard can still fail the neighboring-dwelling distance. The 25-foot requirement cannot be converted to a property-line inset without measuring the neighbor's building location. No normal poultry-keeping permit does not establish a blanket exemption for constructing an accessory structure or complying with zoning restrictions.
spokane-wa: A 5,000-square-foot lot gives an animal-count starting point

Spokane's cited small-domestic-animal provision uses a combined allowance of one qualifying animal or fowl for each 1,000 square feet of parcel area. A 5,000-square-foot lot therefore suggests five under that calculation if the property otherwise qualifies and no other covered animals use the allowance. It is not an automatic promise to keep five hens on every parcel.

Roosters are restricted to the RA district. The published exception from a WSU animal-keeping certificate for chickens is narrower than a general building-permit or zoning waiver. Structures still follow residential accessory-building setbacks, which should be drawn from the correct zone's actual rules.
prescott-valley-az: Utility upgrades can change coop permitting

Prescott Valley's reviewed code allows up to ten chickens per eligible residential lot and prohibits adult male chickens. The cited minimum separation for coops and hutches is one foot from the applicable property or easement line. If an easement is inside the apparent fence boundary, measuring from the fence alone may be inadequate.

The local poultry rules describe a routine no-permit path with an important qualification: a coop containing electrical, mechanical or plumbing installations can trigger a building permit. Before turning a simple shelter into a wired, heated or plumbed structure, verify the current permit classification and land survey rather than assuming the smallest numeric setback approves it.
olympia-wa: Check the lot-size category before choosing a flock

Olympia's revised animal-keeping rule distinguishes parcels of one-quarter acre or less, with up to five female chickens or ducks, from parcels larger than a quarter-acre and under an acre, with up to nine. The larger-lot categories have their own formulas and exceptions; a simple one-bird-per-acre multiplier would therefore misrepresent the code. Roosters and certain loud fowl are excluded.

Enclosures must remain at least ten feet from every property line and also outside applicable zoning setback areas. Meeting the ten-foot measurement alone may be insufficient. The reviewed animal provision does not resolve whether an accessory building permit is required for a specific coop.
frisco-tx: A twelve-bird enclosure cap is not a property-wide guarantee

Frisco's cited ordinance applies a cap of twelve gallinaceous birds in one enclosure; that wording should not be presented as unconditional permission to keep twelve hens on any residential lot. Its rooster clause includes a conditional affirmative defense for premises of at least one acre, which is not a general exemption from nuisance and zoning standards.

Frisco's fowl provisions emphasize enclosed, sanitary housing, but the separate 100-foot rule in the livestock section cannot automatically be transferred to chicken coops. Confirm the operative land-use and structure provisions instead of drawing an invented universal hundred-foot buffer in the planner.
garland-tx: The neighbor's house and the lot line are two different tests

Garland's cited city rule allows up to four qualifying female domestic fowl older than one month and excludes roosters. For a proposed four-hen backyard coop, first mark the nearest neighboring residence and the boundary of any adjoining residentially zoned property, as those are different reference points.

The reviewed provisions use a 30-foot separation from another residence and a separate five-foot buffer for certain pens, runs or cages beside residentially zoned land. Passing five feet from a fence does not prove compliance with the 30-foot house distance. Other building-permit and zoning conditions remain unconfirmed by the poultry section.
minneapolis-mn: Permit tiers do not automatically authorize thirty backyard hens

Minneapolis describes permit tiers for one to six hens, seven to fifteen and sixteen to thirty, but the normal residential six-bird standard remains important. Applicants in higher categories may need additional authorization from Animal Care and Control; choosing the highest fee tier does not itself permit thirty hens at an ordinary home.

The permit application involves neighbor consent, education, zoning approval and inspection before acquiring birds. The coop and run must be behind the principal dwelling and at least twenty feet from a habitable building on an adjacent property, not twenty feet from the shared boundary. A separate rooster permit category is not automatic rooster permission.
madison-wi: Animal licensing and a dwelling-distance test both apply

Madison's official chicken-keeping guidance allows up to eight hens on eligible parcels and does not allow roosters. Keeping chickens requires a municipal chicken license and Wisconsin livestock-premises registration, which should not be confused with one another. Confirm the city's renewal and timing rules before birds arrive.

The covered or fenced chicken enclosure must be at least twenty-five feet from a residential structure on an adjoining lot. Measure the distance to that building, not a made-up property-line inset. Even when the flock count fits, separate zoning, private covenants and construction conditions can affect a particular rear-yard plan.
